questions.stem: A client is admitted with suspected active pulmonary tuberculosis. Which precaution should the nurse implement?

opts.t: Airborne precautions with an N95 respirator and a negative-pressure room
opts.r: Correct. TB spreads by airborne droplet nuclei, requiring an N95 and a negative-pressure (AIIR) room.

opts.t: Droplet precautions with a surgical mask
opts.r: Droplet precautions are insufficient for airborne TB.

opts.t: Contact precautions with a gown and gloves
opts.r: Contact precautions address surface spread, not airborne.

opts.t: Standard precautions only
opts.r: Standard precautions alone do not contain airborne TB.

questions.tip: Airborne ("My Chicken Hz TB"): Measles, Chickenpox/varicella, Herpes zoster (disseminated), TB → N95 + negative-pressure room.

opts.t: A client with bacterial meningitis (Neisseria meningitidis)
opts.r: Correct. Meningococcal meningitis spreads by respiratory droplets — droplet precautions with a surgical mask and private room.

opts.t: A client with active tuberculosis
opts.r: TB requires airborne, not droplet, precautions.

opts.t: A client colonized with MRSA in a wound
opts.r: MRSA requires contact precautions.

opts.t: A client with Clostridioides difficile
opts.r: C. diff requires contact precautions with soap-and-water hand hygiene.

questions.tip: Droplet (surgical mask, ~6 ft): influenza, pertussis, meningitis, mumps, rubella.

questions.stem: A client has a wound infected with methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Which personal protective equipment is required to provide direct care?

opts.t: Gown and gloves
opts.r: Correct. MRSA requires contact precautions — gown and gloves for direct contact.

opts.t: N95 respirator only
opts.r: An N95 is for airborne diseases, not MRSA.

opts.t: Surgical mask and goggles only
opts.r: Droplet/splash gear is not the requirement for contact spread.

opts.t: No PPE beyond hand hygiene
opts.r: MRSA requires contact PPE, not hand hygiene alone.

questions.tip: Contact precautions (gown + gloves): MRSA, VRE, C. diff, RSV, scabies, draining wounds.

questions.stem: After caring for a client with Clostridioides difficile, which hand-hygiene method must the nurse use?

opts.t: Wash with soap and water
opts.r: Correct. C. diff spores are not killed by alcohol; hands must be washed with soap and water.

opts.t: Alcohol-based hand rub
opts.r: Alcohol does not destroy C. diff spores.

opts.t: Hand sanitizer wipes
opts.r: Alcohol wipes are ineffective against spores.

opts.t: Donning a second pair of gloves
opts.r: Gloves do not replace hand washing after spore-forming organisms.

questions.tip: C. diff and norovirus (spores) → SOAP AND WATER, not alcohol rub.

questions.stem: The nurse is removing personal protective equipment after client care. Which item should be removed first?

opts.t: Gloves
opts.r: Correct. Gloves are the most contaminated and are removed first when doffing PPE.

opts.t: Gown
opts.r: The gown is removed after gloves.

opts.t: Mask or respirator
opts.r: The mask is removed last, after leaving the room.

opts.t: Goggles or face shield
opts.r: Eye protection is removed after the gloves.

questions.tip: Doffing order (most→least contaminated): gloves → goggles → gown → mask (mask last, outside the room).

questions.stem: While maintaining a sterile field, which action by the nurse breaks sterile technique?

opts.t: Turning their back on the sterile field
opts.r: Correct. Turning away from the field means it can no longer be observed and is considered contaminated.

opts.t: Holding sterile items above waist level
opts.r: Keeping items above the waist and in view maintains sterility.

opts.t: Considering the outer 1-inch border unsterile
opts.r: Treating the 1-inch border as unsterile is correct practice.

opts.t: Facing the sterile field at all times
opts.r: Facing the field maintains sterility.

questions.tip: Sterile field: keep it in sight and above the waist; 1-inch border and anything below waist = contaminated.

questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has an absolute neutrophil count of 400/mm3. Which intervention is most appropriate?

opts.t: Institute neutropenic (protective) precautions and avoid fresh flowers and raw produce
opts.r: Correct. Severe neutropenia requires protective isolation to reduce infection exposure, including no fresh flowers/raw foods.

opts.t: Place the client on airborne precautions
opts.r: Protective precautions guard the client, not others; airborne isolation is not indicated.

opts.t: Encourage visits from anyone, including those with colds
opts.r: Ill visitors must be screened out to protect the immunocompromised client.

opts.t: Take a rectal temperature every 4 hours
opts.r: Rectal temperatures/suppositories are avoided to prevent mucosal injury and infection.

questions.tip: Neutropenia = PROTECT the client: private room, screen visitors, no fresh flowers/raw foods, no rectal routes.

questions.stem: Which action by the nurse demonstrates correct sharps safety after giving an injection?

opts.t: Dispose of the needle uncapped in a puncture-resistant sharps container
opts.r: Correct. Needles go directly, uncapped, into a puncture-resistant container to prevent injury.

opts.t: Recap the needle using two hands before disposal
opts.r: Recapping — especially two-handed — is a leading cause of needlesticks.

opts.t: Place the needle on the bedside table temporarily
opts.r: Leaving sharps out risks injury to others.

opts.t: Bend the needle before discarding it
opts.r: Bending needles increases exposure risk.

questions.tip: Never recap needles; drop uncapped into the sharps container. Use safety devices.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick injury from a used needle. What is the first action the nurse should take?

opts.t: Wash the site immediately with soap and water
opts.r: Correct. The first step is to wash the exposed site with soap and water, then report and follow the exposure protocol.

opts.t: Apply a tourniquet above the site
opts.r: A tourniquet is not indicated and is not the first step.

opts.t: Squeeze the site to force out blood vigorously
opts.r: Vigorous squeezing is not recommended and can damage tissue.

opts.t: Wait until the end of the shift to report it
opts.r: Exposures must be reported and evaluated immediately for prophylaxis timing.

questions.tip: Needlestick: wash with soap & water first → report immediately → follow post-exposure protocol.

questions.stem: Before administering a medication, how should the nurse correctly identify the client?

opts.t: Use two client identifiers, such as name and date of birth
opts.r: Correct. At least two identifiers (e.g., name and DOB) confirmed against the record are required.

opts.t: Confirm the room and bed number
opts.r: Room/bed numbers change and are not reliable identifiers.

opts.t: Call the client's first name and proceed if they respond
opts.r: A single name response is not a safe identifier.

opts.t: Ask another nurse to point out the client
opts.r: Relying on a pointer is not an approved identification method.

questions.tip: Always verify TWO identifiers (name + DOB or MRN) — never the room number.

questions.stem: Which action best prevents a medication administration error with a high-alert drug such as IV insulin?

opts.t: Have a second nurse independently verify the dose and pump settings
opts.r: Correct. Independent double-checks on high-alert medications reduce serious dosing errors.

opts.t: Prepare several clients' doses at once to save time
opts.r: Batch preparation increases the risk of mix-ups.

opts.t: Rely on memory for the client's usual dose
opts.r: Memory is not a safe substitute for verifying the order.

opts.t: Document the dose before confirming the order
opts.r: Documenting before verification can propagate an error.

questions.tip: High-alert meds (insulin, heparin, opioids, concentrated electrolytes) = independent double-check.

questions.stem: A fire breaks out in a client's room. Using the RACE protocol, what is the nurse's first action?

opts.t: Rescue anyone in immediate danger
opts.r: Correct. RACE begins with Rescue — move anyone in immediate danger to safety first.

opts.t: Activate the fire alarm
opts.r: Alarm is the second step (A), after rescuing those in danger.

opts.t: Confine the fire by closing doors
opts.r: Confine is the third step (C).

opts.t: Extinguish the fire if it is small
opts.r: Extinguish is the final step (E).

questions.tip: RACE: Rescue → Alarm → Confine → Extinguish. (Extinguisher: PASS.)

questions.stem: A child is admitted with varicella (chickenpox). Which room assignment is appropriate?

opts.t: A negative-pressure isolation room on airborne precautions
opts.r: Correct. Varicella requires airborne (and contact) precautions in a negative-pressure room.

opts.t: A shared room with a post-operative child
opts.r: Sharing with a susceptible child risks transmission.

opts.t: A standard room with droplet precautions only
opts.r: Varicella is airborne, not droplet.

opts.t: A room next to the pediatric oncology unit
opts.r: Placing a contagious child near immunocompromised clients is unsafe.

questions.tip: Varicella/measles = airborne + negative pressure. Keep away from immunocompromised clients.

questions.stem: A client reports a latex allergy. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

opts.t: Use latex-free gloves and equipment for all care
opts.r: Correct. A latex-free environment prevents an allergic or anaphylactic reaction.

opts.t: Use latex gloves but change them frequently
opts.r: Any latex contact can trigger a reaction.

opts.t: Premedicate with an antihistamine and use latex products
opts.r: Avoidance, not premedication, is the safe approach.

opts.t: Only avoid latex during invasive procedures
opts.r: Latex must be avoided in all care, not just procedures.

questions.tip: Latex allergy = latex-free everything; cross-reacts with banana, avocado, kiwi.

questions.stem: Which practices are part of standard precautions used with ALL clients? Select all that apply.

opts.t: Perform hand hygiene before and after client contact
opts.r: Correct. Hand hygiene is the foundation of standard precautions for every client.

opts.t: Wear gloves when contact with blood or body fluids is anticipated
opts.r: Correct. Gloves are used whenever exposure to body fluids is possible.

opts.t: Dispose of sharps in a puncture-resistant container
opts.r: Correct. Safe sharps disposal is a standard precaution.

opts.t: Place every client in a private negative-pressure room
opts.r: Incorrect. Negative-pressure rooms are only for airborne precautions, not all clients.

opts.t: Recap all used needles for safety
opts.r: Incorrect. Needles are never recapped.

questions.tip: Standard precautions apply to EVERYONE: hand hygiene, PPE as needed, safe sharps, respiratory etiquette.

questions.stem: A nurse is opening a sterile package to set up a field. Which technique is correct?

opts.t: Open the first flap away from the body, then the sides, then toward the body last
opts.r: Correct. Opening the far flap first and the near flap last avoids reaching over the sterile field.

opts.t: Open the flap closest to the body first
opts.r: Opening the near flap first forces reaching across the field, contaminating it.

opts.t: Reach across the sterile field to arrange items
opts.r: Reaching over a sterile field contaminates it.

opts.t: Place sterile items on the very edge of the field
opts.r: The outer 1-inch border is considered contaminated.

questions.tip: Open sterile wraps: farthest flap first, nearest flap last; never reach over the field.
